results.title: A list or library past 100,000 items can no longer have its permission inheritance broken
results.message: The list holds 4200 items and inherits its permissions, within the 100,000 boundary at which inheritance can no longer be broken.
results.passes_without_resolving: A list holding 99,000 items and growing passes this rule today and loses the ability permanently within weeks, without anything in the report changing to warn about it. The rule measures a position, not a trajectory, and the boundary it describes is the one place where being close to a limit matters more than being past it: once crossed, the option does not come back. Every pass here means "not yet", never "safe".

sources.title: SharePoint limits, Items in lists and libraries
Manage Permission Scopes in SharePoint

results.remediation: Microsoft's guidance is preventive, not corrective: "share large folders before they hit 100,000 items". For a container already past the limit, reducing the count does not restore the ability in every case, and the supported route is to restructure the content across containers that stay below it. Decide whether this container will ever need unique permissions before restructuring, because if the answer is no, no action is required.

because: it passed, and the rule records something the pass does not settle

results.title: A list or library may not hold more than 50,000 unique permission scopes
results.message: The scope count does not settle this list's position relative to the 50,000 limit: either it was not counted, or counting stopped before it could. The evidence beside this finding says which. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: A list at 49,000 scopes passes and is one sharing operation away from the ceiling, and a list at 6,000 passes this rule while sitting well above the number Microsoft recommends for performance. This rule measures only the supported ceiling, and passing it says nothing about whether the list is usable.

sources.title: SharePoint limits, Unique security scopes per list or library
Manage Permission Scopes in SharePoint

results.remediation: Restructure the content so that fewer containers carry their own permissions. A folder shared with three people is one scope; three files shared individually are three. Where a list has grown past the ceiling, the supported route is to split the content across containers rather than to remove permissions one by one, which is slow and rarely finishes.

results.title: A list or library above 5,000 unique permission scopes is past the recommended limit
results.message: The scope count does not settle this list's position relative to the recommended 5,000: either it was not counted, or counting stopped before it could. The evidence beside this finding says which. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: A list at 4,999 scopes passes, and if its access control lists are large it may already be slower than a list at 8,000 with small ones. Microsoft says so explicitly. The count is a proxy for a cost this rule cannot measure, and a pass here is not a statement that the list performs well.

sources.title: SharePoint limits, Unique security scopes per list or library
Manage Permission Scopes in SharePoint

results.remediation: Treat it as a design question rather than a cleanup task. Microsoft's own advice is to design lists to have as few unique permissions as possible, and the cheapest version of that is usually to grant access at a folder rather than at each file inside it.

results.title: No person has changed anything on this site for over a year
results.message: When a person last changed something on this site was not established, so how long it has been is not known. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: Somebody correcting one typo resets this to zero. A single edit satisfies the rule completely and says nothing about whether the site is used, read, or worth keeping, and the sites most worth reviewing are often the ones with one dutiful edit a year.
results.remediation: Find out what it was for before deciding anything. The cheapest outcome is usually to archive it, which keeps the content and takes it out of every list somebody has to read; deleting is a decision that needs an owner, and a site in this state often no longer has one.

results.title: This site carries no sensitivity label and no classification
results.message: Whether this site carries a label or a classification was not established. Neither property could be read, so the site may well be labelled. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: Any label passes. A site labelled Public and a site labelled Highly Confidential are indistinguishable to this rule, and so is a site labelled with whatever came first in the dropdown. It reports that the question was answered, never that the answer was right.

sources.title: Secure by default with Microsoft Purview, Step 3: expand to your entire Microsoft 365 data estate
Use sensitivity labels to protect collaborative workspaces (groups and sites)

results.remediation: Decide first whether the tenant is using container labels at all. If it is not, every site will fail this rule and the finding to act on is the tenant decision, not the site. If it is, the deployment model Microsoft publishes works outward from the sites that matter most rather than through the list in order, and this rule set can produce that list but cannot rank it.

because: the evidence needed to decide this was not available

results.title: This site carries a sensitivity label that could not be resolved to a name
results.message: Whether the label on this site resolves to a name was not established, because the label itself was not read. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: A resolved name passes, and a name is a word. It says nothing about what the label is configured to do: privacy, guest access, the default sharing link and conditional access are all label settings this rule never reads. A site labelled Confidential by a label that enforces nothing passes.

sources.title: Use sensitivity labels to protect collaborative workspaces (groups and sites)

results.remediation: Nothing on the site needs changing. Either the identity that collected the evidence cannot read label definitions, in which case collect again with one that can, or the label was deleted in Purview and the sites still carry its id, in which case the label is the thing to fix and it will be carrying more sites than this one.

because: the evidence needed to decide this was not available

results.title: This group-connected site carries no sensitivity label
results.message: Whether this group-connected site carries a sensitivity label was not established. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: Any label passes, including one configured to set nothing. A label whose protection settings were left empty leaves privacy and guest access exactly where this rule found them and satisfies it completely.

sources.title: Use sensitivity labels to protect collaborative workspaces (groups and sites)
Control external access to resources in Microsoft Entra ID with sensitivity labels

results.remediation: Read the group settings before applying anything. A label sets privacy and external access and locks them, so applying one to a group that is currently configured differently changes the group. That is the point of it and it is also how a labelling exercise removes somebody's access on a Tuesday afternoon.

results.title: The classic publishing infrastructure is enabled on this site
results.message: The enabled features of this web were not read, so whether the classic publishing infrastructure is on is not known. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: A site that never had the publishing feature can still be entirely classic: classic pages, classic web parts, and a custom master page all exist without it. This rule reads one feature identifier and says nothing about how the site is actually built.

sources.title: Moving from publishing sites to communication sites
SPMT supported SharePoint site features, feature identifiers

results.remediation: Read Microsoft's guide before turning anything off. The feature is not the work: the page layouts, the master pages and the content that depends on them are, and disabling the feature without moving them first breaks pages rather than modernising them.

results.title: The site uses a master page other than the ones SharePoint provides
results.message: The master page of this site was not read, so whether it is a provided one is not known. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: A site on seattle.master can be as classic as any other: classic pages, classic web parts, alternate CSS and script editor web parts all survive a default master page. This rule reads one file name.
results.remediation: Find out what it does before deciding anything. A custom master page is sometimes a logo and sometimes a navigation system, and the two are different projects.

results.title: The site loads an alternate stylesheet into every page
results.message: The alternate stylesheet setting was not read, so whether one is loaded is not known. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: An empty setting says nothing about how the site is styled. Themes, custom page layouts, web part properties and script editor web parts all change appearance without this setting being used, and this rule reads only this setting.
results.remediation: Find the file and read it before removing the setting. A stylesheet that hides an element somebody relies on is a support call, not a cleanup.

results.title: A site that allows Anyone links permits access that cannot be attributed
results.message: The sharing capability of this site was not read, so whether it permits Anyone links is not known. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: A site with Anyone links turned off today may hold documents shared that way last year, and those links keep working. Turning the setting off does not revoke what it produced, and this rule reads only the setting.

sources.title: Manage sharing settings for SharePoint and OneDrive, external sharing options
Share within Microsoft OneDrive and SharePoint, sharable links overview

results.remediation: Decide whether this site needs it. Where it does, the controls Microsoft provides are expiry and view-only permission on Anyone links, and both are set per site. Where it does not, a more restrictive capability removes the option without removing external sharing.

results.title: The default sharing link should not be Anyone
results.message: What a person gets when they press Share and change nothing is not settled here: either the setting was not read, or the site sets no default of its own and follows a tenant setting this collection did not read. The evidence beside this finding says which. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: A default of Specific people means nothing about what people actually choose. Somebody who selects the Anyone link every time produces the same result on a site that passes this rule as on one that fails it, and the rule reads only the default.

sources.title: Change the default sharing link type for a site

results.remediation: Set the default to something more restrictive, per site, and leave the Anyone link available for the people who need it. Microsoft's own page describes exactly this arrangement.

results.title: A site should have at least two owners
results.message: The owner count does not settle whether this site has two: either the owners were not collected, or a group among them was not expanded. The evidence beside this finding says which. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: Two owners who are dormant, who have left, or who do not know they own the site satisfy this rule completely. The count is two and nobody is able to act. The rule measures the field, not the availability of a person.
results.remediation: Assign a second accountable owner, and review ownership when people change role. A second owner who does not know they are one is not a second owner: the point is that somebody else can act, not that a field has two values.

because: the evidence needed to decide this was not available

results.title: A site should have at least one administrator who is a person
results.message: The administrators of this site were not read, so whether any of them is an individual account is not known. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: One named administrator who has left the organisation, changed role, or never knew they were named satisfies this rule completely. It reads a field; it cannot read whether the account is active or the person reachable.
results.remediation: Name at least one person alongside the groups, and tell them. The point is not the field: it is that somebody knows the site is theirs to decide about.

because: the evidence needed to decide this was not available

results.title: A site above 90 per cent of its storage quota is close to stopping
results.message: The storage figures for this site were not read, so how full it is remains unknown. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: A site at 40 per cent that doubles every month passes this rule twice before it fails it. The rule reads one number on one day: it measures a level and says nothing about a rate, and the rate is what decides when anybody needs to act.
results.remediation: Raise the quota, or move content out. Which one is right depends on whether the site is growing because it is being used or because nothing has ever been removed from it, and that is a question the numbers here do not answer.

because: the evidence needed to decide this was not available

results.title: A solution is installed at an older version than the catalog holds
results.message: The catalog was not read, so whether any solution is behind the version it holds is not known. This is not a pass.
results.passes_without_resolving: A catalog where every solution is current says nothing about whether any of them still works, is maintained by anybody, or should be there at all. This rule compares two version numbers.
results.remediation: Find out why before upgrading anything. A package that was uploaded and never claimed is sometimes an oversight and sometimes a rollback that nobody wrote down.
